concepts.definition: The place a trail starts, usually with a parking lot, a sign and often a map or register.
concepts.exampleLine: Meet me at the trailhead by 6:30. The lot fills up by eight.

concepts.definition: A hike that goes to a destination and returns the same way you came.
concepts.exampleLine: It's an out-and-back, so the way down is the same view in reverse.

concepts.definition: A route that returns to the start without retracing your steps.
concepts.exampleLine: We're doing the loop clockwise so the big climb is on fresh legs.

concepts.definition: A route with a stem in and out and a loop at the far end.
concepts.exampleLine: It's a lollipop: two miles up the stem, then the loop around the lake.

concepts.definition: A hike that ends somewhere different from where it starts, so you need a shuttle or a ride.
concepts.exampleLine: It's point-to-point, so we're leaving a car at the far trailhead.

concepts.definition: A place where two or more trails meet; the most common spot to take a wrong turn.
concepts.exampleLine: Careful at the junction. Everyone goes left there and it's wrong.

concepts.definition: A hairpin turn that lets a trail climb a steep slope at a gentle, sustainable grade.
concepts.exampleLine: Forty switchbacks. I counted. Twice.

concepts.definition: A painted mark on a tree or rock that keeps you on the trail; a stacked pair often warns of a turn.
concepts.exampleLine: I lost the trail for ten minutes until I spotted a white blaze.

concepts.definition: A small stack of rocks that marks the route where there is no tread, like bare rock or above treeline.
concepts.exampleLine: Follow the cairns across the slab, and please don't build new ones.

concepts.definition: A short side trail off the main route to a viewpoint, lake, water source or campsite.
concepts.exampleLine: There's a spur to the overlook. Ten minutes, totally worth it.

concepts.definition: An unofficial path worn by foot traffic, often shortcuts that cause erosion and confusion.
concepts.exampleLine: That's a social trail. Stay on the real one, it's wrecking the meadow.

concepts.definition: The etiquette of who yields: bikes yield to hikers and horses, hikers yield to horses, and downhill usually yields to uphill.
concepts.exampleLine: I stepped off for the horses. You always yield to the horses.

concepts.definition: Seven principles for minimizing your impact: plan ahead, durable surfaces, waste, leave what you find, campfires, wildlife, other visitors.
concepts.exampleLine: I'm a Leave No Trace person. Pack it in, pack it out.

concepts.definition: Ground that resists damage: maintained trail, rock, gravel, dry grass or snow.
concepts.exampleLine: We rested on the slickrock, it's a durable surface, not the moss.

concepts.definition: Carry all trash, food scraps and toilet paper out with you, including peels and cores.
concepts.exampleLine: Orange peels are trash too. Pack it out.

concepts.definition: A sign-in book or box at a trailhead or pass that logs who went where and when.
concepts.exampleLine: I signed the register. It's how rangers know we were up there.

concepts.definition: A checklist of ten systems (navigation, sun protection, insulation, light, first aid, fire, repair, food, water, shelter) that prepares you to handle an unplanned night out.
concepts.exampleLine: Even for a four-mile hike I carry the ten essentials.

concepts.definition: Wearing several thin layers you can add or remove instead of one thick one, so you can regulate sweat and warmth.
concepts.exampleLine: I never wear one big jacket. Layers, so I can adjust.

concepts.definition: The thin wicking layer against your skin, usually synthetic or merino wool.
concepts.exampleLine: Merino base layer. It doesn't smell after three days.

concepts.definition: The insulating layer, such as fleece or a puffy jacket, that holds in warmth.
concepts.exampleLine: I threw on the puffy at the summit and it was heaven.

concepts.definition: The outer wind and rain layer; it blocks weather but must vent or you sweat inside it.
concepts.exampleLine: Shell's in the pack. The sky looks moody.

concepts.definition: The rule that cotton soaks up water, dries slowly and pulls heat from your body, so avoid it in cool or wet conditions.
concepts.exampleLine: Jeans on a rainy hike? Cotton kills, my friend.

concepts.definition: A fabric's ability to pull sweat off your skin to the outer surface so it can evaporate.
concepts.exampleLine: These socks are wicking. My feet stay dry.

concepts.definition: Shoes that lock your heel, leave room for toes to splay and do not slide on descents; fit matters more than category.
concepts.exampleLine: Wrong-size boots ruined my first hike. Fit is everything.

concepts.definition: A warm, tender patch where friction is starting; the moment to act before it becomes a blister.
concepts.exampleLine: I felt a hot spot at mile three so I stopped and taped it.

concepts.definition: Prevention and treatment: tape hot spots early, keep feet dry, change socks, and cover open blisters properly.
concepts.exampleLine: Tape it before it blisters. Tape early, tape often.

concepts.definition: Adjustable poles that reduce load on knees on descents and add balance on rough or wet ground.
concepts.exampleLine: Poles saved my knees on the descent.

concepts.definition: A 10 to 30 liter pack carrying the day's essentials, food, water and layers.
concepts.exampleLine: Twenty-liter daypack, snacks on the hip belt.

concepts.definition: A hands-free light carried on every hike, including day hikes, in case you finish after dark.
concepts.exampleLine: I always throw a headlamp in, even if I'll be back by noon.

concepts.definition: Lightweight protection like a bivy or space blanket that lets you survive an unplanned night.
concepts.exampleLine: There's an emergency bivy at the bottom of my pack, just in case.

concepts.definition: Sunscreen, sunglasses, hat and sun-covering clothing; UV rises with elevation and reflects off snow and water.
concepts.exampleLine: Sunburn above treeline is no joke. Hat and SPF, always.

concepts.definition: Supplies for blisters, cuts, sprains and allergic reactions, matched to the trip length and your training.
concepts.exampleLine: I carry a small first aid kit, tape and blister pads mostly.

concepts.definition: A fire starter for emergencies plus a small kit (knife, tape, cord) to fix gear on the trail.
concepts.exampleLine: Duct tape wrapped on my poles. It fixes everything.

concepts.definition: A rule of thumb of about half a liter per hour in moderate weather, more in heat or steep terrain.
concepts.exampleLine: About half a liter an hour. More when it's hot.

concepts.definition: Making backcountry water safe by filtering, chemical treatment, UV or boiling.
concepts.exampleLine: I filter everything. Even the pretty streams.

concepts.definition: A microscopic parasite in natural water that causes severe stomach illness; filters and treatment stop it.
concepts.exampleLine: Clear water still has giardia. I've seen the hospital bills.

concepts.definition: Salts you lose in sweat, sodium especially; replace them on long or hot hikes.
concepts.exampleLine: I drop an electrolyte tab in one bottle every hot day.

concepts.definition: Dangerously low blood sodium from drinking lots of plain water without salt, causing confusion and nausea.
concepts.exampleLine: Chugging plain water all day isn't safe. Salt matters.

concepts.definition: Hiking burns roughly 300 to 500 calories an hour; snacking a little every hour beats a big meal.
concepts.exampleLine: Snack every hour, not just at lunch.

concepts.definition: Hitting the wall when your energy stores run out, producing weakness, irritability and slowness.
concepts.exampleLine: I bonked at mile eight. Forgot to eat.

concepts.definition: Calorie-dense food that survives a pack: nuts, bars, jerky, cheese, dried fruit, tortillas.
concepts.exampleLine: Tortillas and peanut butter is the best trail lunch.

concepts.definition: Headache, nausea and fatigue from going up faster than your body adapts, usually above about 8,000 feet.
concepts.exampleLine: I had a headache at the pass. Altitude, I think.

concepts.definition: Letting your body adapt to elevation by ascending gradually and sleeping lower than your high point.
concepts.exampleLine: We're spending a night at 8,000 feet to acclimatize first.

concepts.definition: A spectrum from cramps to heat exhaustion to heatstroke, an emergency with confusion and hot dry skin.
concepts.exampleLine: We started at dawn because the canyon is dangerous by noon.

concepts.definition: Dark urine, headache, dizziness, dry mouth and unusual fatigue.
concepts.exampleLine: My urine was dark, so I doubled my water.

concepts.definition: The total climbing on a route, adding every uphill, not just the difference between start and top.
concepts.exampleLine: Only six miles, but two thousand feet of gain.

concepts.definition: The steepness of a slope as rise over run in percent.
concepts.exampleLine: The grade steepens to fifteen percent past the falls.

concepts.definition: A planning formula: one hour per three miles plus one hour per two thousand feet of climbing.
concepts.exampleLine: By Naismith's rule, we're looking at four hours up.

concepts.definition: Moving time counts walking only; total time includes breaks, photos and lunch.
concepts.exampleLine: Three hours moving, but five with breaks and views.

concepts.definition: How fast you cover ground, typically about two miles an hour on moderate terrain, less on steep or rough terrain.
concepts.exampleLine: On steep trail we averaged a mile and a half an hour.

concepts.definition: Labels like easy or strenuous that are subjective and not standardized across apps and agencies.
concepts.exampleLine: They call it moderate. It felt strenuous to me.

concepts.definition: The Yosemite Decimal System's classes 1 to 5, from walking to roped climbing.
concepts.exampleLine: It's class 2, a little hands-on scrambling near the top.

concepts.definition: Steep drop-offs beside your route where a fall would be serious.
concepts.exampleLine: The exposure on the ridge was intense.

concepts.definition: A trail has maintained tread; a route follows a line across terrain without one.
concepts.exampleLine: It's a route, not a trail. You need to navigate.

concepts.definition: Whether streams and springs are actually flowing; many are seasonal and can be dry.
concepts.exampleLine: The spring at mile six may be dry in September.

concepts.definition: A line on a map connecting points of equal elevation.
concepts.exampleLine: Those contours are so tight that the slope has to be brutal.

concepts.definition: The vertical distance in elevation between adjacent contour lines.
concepts.exampleLine: Forty foot contour interval on this map.

concepts.definition: A darker contour line, usually every fifth, labeled with its elevation.
concepts.exampleLine: Follow the bold index contours to read the height.

concepts.definition: A ridge is a long crest of high ground; a spur is a smaller ridge sticking out from it. Contours bend down-slope, away from higher ground.
concepts.exampleLine: We're walking the ridge, then dropping down the spur.

concepts.definition: A low point on a ridge between two higher points, appearing as an hourglass on a map.
concepts.exampleLine: The saddle between the two peaks is where the trail crosses.

concepts.definition: A valley or draw where water runs; contours form Vs that point uphill.
concepts.exampleLine: Follow the drainage down and you'll hit the creek.

concepts.definition: Contour lines that bunch together or merge, signaling very steep or vertical ground.
concepts.exampleLine: The contours merge here. That's a cliff, not a trail.

concepts.definition: The ratio of map distance to real distance; on a 1:24,000 map, one inch is 2,000 feet.
concepts.exampleLine: On a one to twenty-four thousand map, an inch is two thousand feet.

concepts.definition: The key that explains map symbols such as trails, roads, water and vegetation.
concepts.exampleLine: I checked the legend to see if that dashed line was a trail.

concepts.definition: Three norths: the geographic pole, where a compass points, and the map's grid lines.
concepts.exampleLine: Compass north isn't map north. Check the declination.

concepts.definition: The angle between true north and magnetic north at your location, which changes by place and year.
concepts.exampleLine: Declination here is about ten degrees east, so I adjusted.

concepts.definition: A direction expressed in degrees from north, from 0 to 360.
concepts.exampleLine: Take a bearing of ninety, due east, to the lake.

concepts.definition: A linear feature such as a stream, ridge or road that you can follow to stay oriented.
concepts.exampleLine: I used the creek as a handrail all the way down.

concepts.definition: A feature that tells you that you have gone too far, like a road or river past your target.
concepts.exampleLine: The road is my catching feature. If I hit it, I overshot.

concepts.definition: A recorded breadcrumb line of where you have been, which can be followed back.
concepts.exampleLine: I saved my GPS track so I can retrace it.

concepts.definition: Map areas downloaded to a phone so navigation works without signal.
concepts.exampleLine: I downloaded the offline map before losing signal.

concepts.definition: A saved point such as a trailhead, junction or water source.
concepts.exampleLine: I dropped a waypoint at the car.

concepts.definition: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan: the first response when you are unsure where you are.
concepts.exampleLine: When I get turned around, I do STOP. Sit, breathe, look at the map.

concepts.definition: Estimating position from a known start, direction, speed and time.
concepts.exampleLine: Forty minutes at two miles an hour, so about a mile and a third along.

concepts.definition: Deliberately aiming to one side of a target on a linear feature so you know which way to turn.
concepts.exampleLine: I aimed off to the left so I'd know which way to turn at the creek.

concepts.definition: Air cools about 3 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit per thousand feet of elevation gain.
concepts.exampleLine: It's 70 at the trailhead, but the summit will be 50.

concepts.definition: A forecast for an exact map location and elevation rather than a nearby town.
concepts.exampleLine: I checked the point forecast for the summit, not the town.

concepts.definition: Mountain storms that build in the afternoon after morning heating.
concepts.exampleLine: Storms build after noon here, so we go early.

concepts.definition: Starting before dawn to be off exposed terrain before afternoon weather.
concepts.exampleLine: Alpine start at 4 AM to be off the peak by noon.

concepts.definition: Leave summits and ridges early, avoid lone trees, spread out the group and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
concepts.exampleLine: When thunder roars, get off the ridge.

concepts.definition: How much colder wind makes exposed skin feel; it does not lower the actual air temperature.
concepts.exampleLine: Fifty degrees with wind gusts feels like thirty-five.

concepts.definition: A forecast rating of heat danger that accounts for temperature, humidity and sun.
concepts.exampleLine: The heat risk is extreme today, so we're hiking at dawn.

concepts.definition: Dangerous cooling of the body core, showing as shivering, fumbling and confusion, even above freezing.
concepts.exampleLine: It was 45 and rainy. Hypothermia happens in that too.

concepts.definition: A sudden, violent rise in water from rain that may fall miles away, especially dangerous in canyons and washes.
concepts.exampleLine: Rain upstream can flood a slot canyon while it's sunny above.

concepts.definition: A 0 to 500 scale of air pollution; wildfire smoke can push it into unhealthy ranges.
concepts.exampleLine: The AQI is 160 from smoke, so we're skipping the hike.

concepts.definition: A fire-weather alert for warm, dry, windy conditions when fires spread fast.
concepts.exampleLine: There's a red flag warning, so no campfires and no risk.

concepts.definition: Accumulated snow that lingers on high trails into summer, hiding tread and making steep slopes hazardous.
concepts.exampleLine: The pass will still have snowpack until July.

concepts.definition: A stretch of settled weather long enough to complete a plan.
concepts.exampleLine: We got a weather window from eight to two.

concepts.definition: A pre-set clock time at which you head back regardless of how close the summit is.
concepts.exampleLine: Our turnaround is one o'clock, summit or not.

concepts.definition: Working back from sunset using pace, distance and buffer to know when you must turn around.
concepts.exampleLine: Sunset is 6:42, so we start back by 3:30.

concepts.definition: The urge to push on toward the goal and ignore warning signs.
concepts.exampleLine: I got summit fever and ignored the clouds. Mistake.

concepts.definition: Pressing on because of effort already spent rather than the risk ahead.
concepts.exampleLine: We'd come so far, but the trail was too icy to continue.

concepts.definition: Telling someone your route, group and return time, and when to call for help.
concepts.exampleLine: I left my trip plan with a friend, with a call-out time.

concepts.definition: Extra time, water, food and daylight beyond the plan.
concepts.exampleLine: I plan for margin, an extra hour and extra snacks.

concepts.definition: The rule that the slowest hiker sets the speed and no one gets left behind.
concepts.exampleLine: We hike at the pace of the slowest person.

concepts.definition: Distress signaling such as three whistle blasts, three flashes or three fires.
concepts.exampleLine: Three whistle blasts means help.

concepts.definition: A device that texts or sends SOS via satellite when no cell service exists.
concepts.exampleLine: My inReach lets me message from the middle of nowhere.

concepts.definition: Medical training for situations where help is hours away.
concepts.exampleLine: I did a wilderness first aid course last spring.

concepts.definition: Crossing a stream safely: scout, cross early, unbuckle the hip belt and face upstream; or skip it.
concepts.exampleLine: It was knee deep and fast, so we turned around.

concepts.definition: Standard precautions: keep distance, do not feed, make noise in bear country, know local guidance.
concepts.exampleLine: We saw a bear a hundred yards off and gave it space.

concepts.definition: A hard-sided container that keeps food from bears in areas that require it.
concepts.exampleLine: The park requires bear canisters overnight.

concepts.definition: Cell coverage in the backcountry is patchy at best; plan as if there is none.
concepts.exampleLine: I don't count on signal out there. I download the map.

concepts.definition: The weight of your pack without food, water and fuel.
concepts.exampleLine: My base weight is twelve pounds.

concepts.definition: The three heaviest items: pack, shelter and sleep system.
concepts.exampleLine: I dropped two pounds just by swapping my big three.

concepts.definition: A philosophy of carrying very little, typically a base weight under ten pounds.
concepts.exampleLine: I'm ultralight, so no camp chair.

concepts.definition: The debate: light, breathable trail runners versus boots with ankle support and durability.
concepts.exampleLine: I'm a trail-runner convert. Boots feel like ankle prisons.

concepts.definition: Letting shoes get wet and drain rather than fight to keep them dry.
concepts.exampleLine: I splash through creeks now. My shoes dry while I walk.

concepts.definition: The perennial debate over reliance on batteries versus paper; the sensible answer is both.
concepts.exampleLine: Phone is my main, paper map is the backup.

concepts.definition: Squeeze, gravity, pump and UV each trade speed, weight and reliability.
concepts.exampleLine: I use a squeeze filter. It's light, but it can freeze.

concepts.definition: Moving quickly with a very light pack, mixing hiking and running.
concepts.exampleLine: We're fastpacking it in two days. It's a run and a hike.

concepts.definition: A trail-culture motto: everyone chooses their own pace, gear and style.
concepts.exampleLine: Hike your own hike, whatever works for you.

concepts.definition: A short trip to test gear before a big one.
concepts.exampleLine: We did a shakedown hike to test my new pack.

concepts.definition: Hiking a long trail end to end in one continuous journey.
concepts.exampleLine: She's thru-hiking the whole Appalachian Trail.

concepts.definition: Completing a long trail in pieces over time.
concepts.exampleLine: I've section hiked about half of it.

concepts.definition: A nickname a hiker earns or is given on the trail.
concepts.exampleLine: My trail name is Sherpa, because I carry everyone's snacks.

concepts.definition: Unexpected kindness for hikers, like free food or a ride.
concepts.exampleLine: There was trail magic at the road, with cold soda and hot dogs.

concepts.definition: Completing the Appalachian, Pacific Crest and Continental Divide Trails.
concepts.exampleLine: He's got two of the Triple Crown and needs the CDT.

concepts.definition: Northbound and southbound thru-hikers.
concepts.exampleLine: I'm a NOBO. I start in Georgia in March.

concepts.definition: A zero is a rest day with no hiking miles; a nero is a near-zero day with few.
concepts.exampleLine: I'm taking a zero in town to rest my feet.

concepts.definition: The enormous appetite thru-hikers develop after weeks of long days.
concepts.exampleLine: Hiker hunger hit and I ate two pizzas.

concepts.definition: Buying or receiving food and supplies along a long route.
concepts.exampleLine: Next resupply is in town, four days ahead.

concepts.definition: Fastest known time: an informal record for a set route.
concepts.exampleLine: He's chasing an FKT on the loop.

concepts.definition: Trying to summit every peak on a list, like 14ers or the Adirondack 46.
concepts.exampleLine: I'm peakbagging the 14ers, and I've done nine.

concepts.definition: The 1964 U.S. law creating a system of protected wilderness areas where motors and permanent structures are prohibited.
concepts.exampleLine: It's designated wilderness, so no bikes and no motors.

concepts.definition: Trekking between lodges or huts instead of carrying a tent.
concepts.exampleLine: We're doing a hut-to-hut in the Alps.

concepts.definition: A trail family, the group of hikers who bond on a long trail.
concepts.exampleLine: My tramily and I hiked together for weeks.

concepts.definition: The elevation above which trees cannot grow, marking a change to exposed alpine terrain.
concepts.exampleLine: Above treeline there is no shelter from storms.

concepts.definition: Loose rock: talus is boulder-sized, scree is smaller and slides underfoot.
concepts.exampleLine: The scree slope slid with every step.

concepts.definition: A living crust of organisms in desert soil, easily destroyed by footsteps.
concepts.exampleLine: Don't bust the crust, stay on the trail.

concepts.definition: Glacial landforms: a bowl carved in a mountainside and the ridge of debris a glacier left.
concepts.exampleLine: The lake sits in a cirque beneath a moraine.

concepts.definition: Stunted, wind-twisted trees at the edge of treeline.
concepts.exampleLine: Those twisted krummholz trees are hundreds of years old.

concepts.definition: Inspecting your body after hikes in tick country and using repellent and treated clothing.
concepts.exampleLine: I do a tick check after every hike.

concepts.definition: A plant with three-leaved clusters that causes an itchy rash on contact.
concepts.exampleLine: Leaves of three, let it be.

concepts.definition: Sinking deeply into soft snow with each step.
concepts.exampleLine: We were postholing to our knees by noon.

concepts.definition: Slip-on traction for icy trails.
concepts.exampleLine: Bring microspikes. That north slope is icy till June.

concepts.definition: A random draw that allocates limited permits for popular hikes.
concepts.exampleLine: I won the lottery for the Wave, I can't believe it.

concepts.definition: A reservation for a window of entry into busy parks to limit crowding.
concepts.exampleLine: We need a timed-entry reservation for the park.

concepts.definition: A permit to camp or hike in a protected backcountry zone, often with quotas.
concepts.exampleLine: We got the backcountry permit for two nights.

concepts.definition: Free or paid shuttles that carry visitors to trailheads where parking is limited.
concepts.exampleLine: We take the shuttle to the trailhead, no parking.

concepts.definition: The federal recreation pass covering entrance fees at national parks and other federal lands.
concepts.exampleLine: I bought the annual pass, it paid for itself in three visits.

concepts.definition: A deep, narrow canyon carved by water, hazardous during rain nearby.
concepts.exampleLine: The slot canyon glowed, but we watched the sky.

concepts.definition: Water stashed ahead on a desert route for later use.
concepts.exampleLine: I cached water at the trailhead for the return.

concepts.definition: A 1 to 5 rating from low to extreme published by avalanche centers.
concepts.exampleLine: Danger is level 3, considerable, so we're avoiding steep slopes.

concepts.definition: An overhanging shelf of wind-packed snow on a ridge that can collapse.
concepts.exampleLine: Stay back from the cornice, you can't tell where it ends.

concepts.definition: A recent, human account of conditions like snow, mud, closures or blowdowns.
concepts.exampleLine: The trail report says the creek crossing is high.

concepts.definition: An official closure of an area due to wildfire risk or activity.
concepts.exampleLine: The forest is closed because of the fire.

concepts.definition: The best period for a hike, like wildflower bloom, fall color or snowmelt.
concepts.exampleLine: Peak wildflowers hit in mid July.

concepts.definition: Official notices about hazards or closed trails, published by land agencies.
concepts.exampleLine: I checked the park alerts before we left.

facts.summary: Permit lotteries, timed entry, shuttles, passes and park alerts.
Heat, dry routes, water caches, slot canyons and flash floods.
Treeline, altitude, storms, late snow and avalanche awareness (not training).

payload.title: Sunrise on the ridge

exchanges.theirMessage: Just got back from the ridge. Caught sunrise, so worth the 4 AM alarm.

replies.text: 4 AM start? That's real alpine-start dedication. How was the light?
replies.theirResponse: Right? The whole valley went pink. Most people never see it.
replies.coachNote: Names the idea, then asks about her experience.

replies.text: Wow, that's early. Was it cold?
replies.theirResponse: Freezing at first, then perfect once the sun came up.
replies.coachNote: Fine, but you skipped the interesting part.

replies.text: I could totally do that, I'm basically a mountaineer.
replies.theirResponse: Ha, sure. Okay.
replies.coachNote: Do not fake a level of experience you do not have.

exchanges.theirMessage: Honestly the descent was rough on my knees though.

replies.text: Did you have poles? I hear they take a lot of load off on descents.
replies.theirResponse: Yes! Poles saved me on the way down. Want to try mine sometime?
replies.coachNote: Shows you learned something and invites a next step.

replies.text: Ouch. Did you ice them after?
replies.theirResponse: Yep, a bag of frozen peas.

replies.text: Just walk faster, it hurts less.
replies.theirResponse: That is not how that works.
replies.coachNote: Advice without knowledge is a friction point.

payload.closingNote: Asking about the moment beats claiming the skill.

payload.title: Saturday plan

exchanges.theirMessage: Want to do the lake loop Saturday? About 7 miles, 1,500 ft of gain.

replies.text: Sounds great. I'm newer to this, so what pace should I expect? I'll bring snacks and layers.
replies.theirResponse: Perfect. We'll keep it easy. Bring water too.
replies.coachNote: Honesty about your level plus a preparedness signal.

replies.text: Sure, sounds fun!
replies.theirResponse: Great, it's a date.
replies.coachNote: Warm, but you did not learn what you are signing up for.

replies.text: Easy, that's nothing. I could do 15.
replies.theirResponse: Ha, okay, we'll see on Saturday.
replies.coachNote: Overpromising is how people end up in trouble on trail.

exchanges.theirMessage: We should leave by 8 and set a 2 PM turnaround to beat the storms.

replies.text: Love a turnaround time. Should I check the forecast tonight?
replies.theirResponse: Yes please. I'll check too.
replies.coachNote: You respect the plan and offer to help.

replies.text: Okay, 8 it is.
replies.theirResponse: Cool.

replies.text: Turnaround? We'll see how we feel up there.
replies.theirResponse: I'd rather set it now, when we're calm.
replies.coachNote: Summit fever starts with 'we'll see how we feel'.

payload.closingNote: Plans made when you're calm keep you safe when you're not.

payload.title: Base weight brag

exchanges.theirMessage: My base weight is finally down to eleven pounds!

replies.text: Eleven! What was the biggest swap, the pack, the shelter or the sleeping bag?
replies.theirResponse: The shelter. Went to a tarp. I'm in love.
replies.coachNote: Uses the big three idea as a genuine question.

replies.text: Nice! Is that light?
replies.theirResponse: Very. Most people carry double that.
replies.coachNote: Honest, but you can do better.

replies.text: Mine's like 40 pounds and I don't care.
replies.theirResponse: Haha, well, your knees might.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing what she cares about closes the topic.

exchanges.theirMessage: It costs some comfort though. No camp chair.

replies.text: Worth it for the miles? Or do you miss it?
replies.theirResponse: Worth it. I sit on my pack.
replies.coachNote: Explores the trade-off she cares about.

replies.text: Comfort's overrated.
replies.theirResponse: Ha, not always.
replies.coachNote: Agreeing without asking why is empty.

replies.text: So basically you are suffering on purpose.
replies.theirResponse: It's a choice, not suffering!
replies.coachNote: Mocking the hobby is not curiosity.

payload.closingNote: Ask about trade-offs. Every gear choice is one.

payload.title: Storm nerves

exchanges.theirMessage: The forecast says 50% storms after noon and I'm second-guessing Saturday.

replies.text: Good instinct. Could we start earlier or pick a lower trail?
replies.theirResponse: That's smart. A lower loop would do it.
